messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 30
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Software Engineer
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
  pcl5: 46

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Gustatory (Taste): A specific taste associated with the event, Olfactory (Sweat/Body): Sweat or body odour, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Threat: Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep, Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
  Memory: Confused Sequence: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order, Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Blocked Before Complete: I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Priya Nair is a thirty-year-old South Asian woman who works as a software engineer at a mid-sized technology firm in the Seattle area. She is married, describes her husband as supportive, and came to her first appointment carrying a careful composure that only partially concealed how exhausted she was. She had delayed seeking help for years, she explained, because she had told herself that what happened in her childhood was over, that she had survived it, and that revisiting it would accomplish nothing. What finally brought her in was a morning at work, three months ago, when a colleague walked past her desk smelling of stale sweat and last night's alcohol, and Priya found herself unable to type, unable to speak, and certain — in a way that felt entirely physical rather than rational — that she was no longer in an open-plan office in Seattle but somewhere much smaller and much more dangerous.

Priya grew up in a household in New Jersey where her father's drinking was the organizing fact of family life. On the evenings he came home already drunk, the atmosphere in the house changed before he even opened the door — she would sometimes smell him before she heard him, the sharp, fermented odour of alcohol cutting through the hallway. What followed on the worst nights was physical: he would strike her, most often with his hands, sometimes with whatever was near him, and the episodes would end only when he exhausted himself or passed out. One detail Priya returned to obliquely, and could not yet hold in full — something about food, a meal, a specific taste that was present on one of the worst occasions. She could not say more than that. When the memory began to surface she found herself pushing it away before it could complete itself, and when she tried to reconstruct the sequence of events from those years she found the chronology genuinely disordered, one night bleeding into another, cause and effect scrambled in ways that disoriented her even as she attempted to describe them.

In the years after she left home for university, Priya built a life that looked, from the outside, entirely intact. She was technically skilled, professionally successful, and had married a man who was, by every measure she could identify, nothing like her father. And yet the years had quietly accumulated their own architecture of management. She had come to believe that the only safe state was a vigilant one, and so she was never fully at rest. In the evenings, before she could attempt sleep, she moved through the apartment checking that the front door was locked, then the windows, then the door again — a circuit she completed multiple times, not because she doubted the locks but because the doubt returned the moment she stepped away from them. Sleep, when it came, came late and broke often. At work, the open-plan floor — the proximity of colleagues, the unpredictability of who might walk past and carrying what smell — had become a source of sustained, low-grade difficulty. After the morning three months ago, she had begun requesting to work from home as often as her team structure permitted, citing focus and productivity. Her manager had accommodated her, but she was aware that her increasing physical absence from the office had started to affect her visibility on collaborative projects, and that a promotion she had been tracking quietly was moving toward someone else.

At home, even on evenings when her husband was present and the apartment was locked and quiet, Priya found she could not settle into the safety she knew, intellectually, was real. She was certain that the feeling of ease other people described — simply sitting, simply being — was not available to her in the same way, and she had stopped expecting it.

What she is most afraid of, sitting in the consulting room, is that fully remembering what happened will confirm something she has worked hard not to articulate: that the worst nights were worse than she has allowed herself to know. What she is hoping for, more tentatively, is that it might eventually be possible to walk through her own office without bracing herself against the air.
